paragraphs.heading: The rock of the continents
paragraphs.text: Continental crust is a layer of rock of three main kinds, igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary, that makes up the continents and the shallow seabed along their coasts, called continental shelves. Most of it is dry land above sea level. Zealandia is an exception: 94% of that region of continental crust lies under the Pacific Ocean. The layer is sometimes called sial because it is richer in aluminium silicates than oceanic crust.

paragraphs.heading: Thick and light
paragraphs.text: Its average density is about 2.83 g/cm³, lighter than the mantle at around 3.3 g/cm³ and than oceanic crust at about 2.9 g/cm³. At 25 to 70 km thick, it is also much thicker than oceanic crust, which averages around 7 to 10 km. Continental crust covers about 41% of Earth's surface and holds about 70% of the volume of Earth's crust.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters for life
paragraphs.text: Since this crust lies mainly above the sea, it made it possible for life on land to evolve from life in the sea. It also provides wide stretches of shallow water, the continental shelves and shallow seas called epeiric seas. There, complex life could become established in the early Paleozoic, during what is now called the Cambrian explosion.

paragraphs.heading: How it is made
paragraphs.text: All continental crust comes in the end from melts that come from the mantle, mainly basalt. Those melts change through fractional differentiation, and older continental crust is also remelted and mixed in; the first process is thought to matter more. This happens mostly at magmatic arcs linked to subduction. Partial melting of oceanic crust at subduction zones sends lighter material up as magma that builds volcanoes. Island arcs and seamounts can also crash into a continent's side and be added to it.

paragraphs.heading: Built mostly long ago
paragraphs.text: There is little sign of continental crust from before 3.5 billion years ago. About 20% of today's volume had formed by 3.0 billion years ago. Between 3.0 and 2.5 billion years ago growth was fast, and about 60% of the present volume formed. The last 20% has formed during the 2.5 billion years since.

paragraphs.heading: A lasting record
paragraphs.text: Continental crust is long-lived, while oceanic crust is short-lived. Because continental crust is less dense, when the two meet at subduction zones it is usually the oceanic crust that sinks back into the mantle. Continental crust is rarely subducted. That makes it, with the rock layers on and in it, the best archive of Earth's history.

paragraphs.heading: Mountain roots and rifts
paragraphs.text: Mountain height usually tracks crust thickness. Collisions and subduction squeeze the crust and make it thicker, and its buoyancy pushes it up. Beneath the range this forms a keel, or mountain root, where the crust is thickest. The thinnest continental crust lies in rift zones, where faulting thins it until it splits apart and oceanic crust takes its place.
